newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibia might scrap project to drain Okavango river.
newsitem.headline: Namibia might scrap project to drain Okavango river.

text.p: Namibia said on Friday it could drop a controversial plan to drain water from the Okavango river after recent good rains eased the country's decade-long drought.
Conservationists in next-door Botswana, into which the river runs, have opposed the scheme, fearing above all that it will disrupt the delicate ecosystem of its unique Okavango Delta.

"Basically, we now have enough water to see us through for two rainy seasons, enough to supply the demand up to the end of March 1999. So the emergency need to build the pipeline has been removed," said Piet Heyns, a Namibian delegate to the Permanent Okavango River Basin Commission with Botswana and Angola.
All three countries met in the Namibian capital, Windhoek, on Thursday for fresh talks on the plan.
The project proposed to tap up to 17 million cubic metres (600 million cubic feet) a year from the river out of a total of 10 billion cubic metres (350 billion cubic feet) that flows into the delta.
Heyns said dams in Namibia were slowly filling up.
"At present the dams in the central region are filled to 28 percent of their total capacity, which is approximately 40 million cubic metres.
"Half of that evaporates over the next two years and consumption is 18 million cubic metres, so we're marginally safe and the emergency project is not such an emergency any more."
The commission, launched in September 1994, said in a statement on Friday that Namibia had briefed the other countries during the meeting on the current dam inflows.
"Namibia....indicated that the situation would now be reviewed," the statement said.
Heyns said a technical study on the proposed project would be tabled in March, after which it was up to the Namibian government to make a final decision.
The Okavango rises in Angola and flows across Namibia's Caprivi Strip before entering Botswana. At least 75 percent of Botswana's tourism revenues come from the delta.
